key_features.classic_presentation: Acute cholecystitis presents with SUDDEN ONSET severe right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain that is CONSTANT (not colicky like biliary colic). Pain often begins 30 minutes to 2 hours AFTER A FATTY MEAL (fried foods, heavy meals) and lasts >6 hours (unlike biliary colic which lasts <6 hours). The pain RADIATES TO THE RIGHT SHOULDER OR SCAPULA (referred pain from phrenic nerve). Pain severity is typically 7-10/10, sharp or aching. Onset is usually within 12-48 hours (acute, not chronic). Key associated symptoms: NAUSEA AND VOMITING are very common, fever (100.5-102°F) develops within 12-24 hours, and patients may have right-sided tenderness with MURPHY'S SIGN (inspiratory arrest during RUQ palpation). Location: Pain is precisely localized to RUQ, just below the right rib cage. Patients may have had PRIOR EPISODES of similar but shorter-lasting pain (biliary colic from gallstones). Key positives: Pain worse with deep breathing or movement, may have jaundice (yellowing) if common bile duct involved, anorexia. Key negatives: Diarrhea is uncommon. Left-sided pain rules out cholecystitis. Pain that completely resolves within 1-2 hours suggests biliary colic, not cholecystitis.

red_flags: High fever >102.5°F with rigors - suggests gangrenous cholecystitis or ascending cholangitis
Jaundice with confusion or sepsis - ascending cholangitis, needs urgent ERCP
Severe RUQ pain with hypotension - gallbladder perforation or septic shock, call 911
Elderly or diabetic patients - higher risk of gangrenous cholecystitis and perforation
